claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/
The post at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
SST was originally built on AWS CDK, which allows defining infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem; Pulumi offers real-time debugging, faster direct execution, and cross-cloud secrets support versus CDK's slower CloudFormation-based deployment.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management.
Ion is the code name for a new SST engine that deploys components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi for its providers and deployment engine and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises.
CDK and CloudFormation generate an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud; the engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for deploying to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code in a single `sst.config.ts` file and `sst deploy` provisions end to end.
Through 2023 SST's provisioning layer was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation; in late 2023 the team began a rewrite code-named Ion.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.
The SST team has repeatedly described its architecture as built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: 'Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).'

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: 'When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources.'
SST docs 'What is SST' say: 'SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi.'
Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' states SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST constructs.
Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article says: 'You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now.'

SST's platform package.json depends on @pulumi/pulumi plus @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls and @pulumiverse/vercel as direct dependencies, in the anomalyco/sst repository (formerly sst/sst).
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, and the provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Nitric's docs state 'all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments', with official Nitric providers built on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang's pulumi-defang provider takes a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`; Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package gets roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has a larger GitHub following (stars) than SST itself.
SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
The team's attention to opencode hasn't changed SST's release cadence.
Writing a correct provisioning engine is a bigger project than it looks; the Pulumi engine is production-grade.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides central guardrails, and components share infrastructure patterns across an organization.
The post 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' exists at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ and tells the story of SST's move off CDK.
